scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. So the user is asking whether refusing to loan their brother vacation money is morally acceptable. The question is to answer 0 or 1 based on moral acceptability.

First, I need to understand the situation. The person (21F) has been saving for a vacation post-graduation, about $2800 saved so far. Her brother (30M) is living with parents, going back to school, and wants to borrow her vacation fund for a trip to Japan. She refused, and he's upset, saying it's unfair because she got to go on trips with parents more, and he's been struggling.

Now, evaluating moral acceptability. Key points: she saved her own money over time, specifically for her own future vacation. The brother is asking to borrow it, but she has reasons to doubt he'll pay back. He's described as "horrible with money," even though he makes similar income. She doesn't pay rent but does buy groceries, etc., while he doesn't pay rent or groceries. Parents have been helping him financially already.

Moral considerations: Ownership of personal savings. If she saved it herself, it's her money. She's not obligated to lend it, especially if there's a risk he won't repay. The brother's arguments about fairness—like her getting more family trips or him having to work—might be emotional but don't necessarily override her right to her own savings. Also, the fact that she's saving for her own goals, which she's worked towards, is important. Lending money to someone who's bad with money could lead to her losing it, which would harm her own plans.

In terms of moral acceptability, generally, people have the right to control their own finances. Unless there's a specific obligation (like a prior agreement), refusing to lend money is usually acceptable. The brother's complaints about fairness don't change the fact that the money is hers. Parents have been helping him, so he shouldn't expect her to step in. Also, she's in school and saving for her future, which is a valid reason to keep her savings.

Possible counterarguments: Maybe family should help each other, but that's not a moral obligation unless there's a clear duty. In many cultures, family support is expected, but in this case, she's not responsible for his financial situation. He's an adult, living with parents, but she's also contributing to her own expenses. Her saving is for her own future, not something she's hoarding selfishly.

So, morally, refusing is acceptable. She's not required to lend money, especially when there's a risk of non-repayment and her own plans are at stake. The brother's anger doesn't make it wrong for her to say no.

Therefore, the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable).
